description: this is our team We are a Colombo team taking on the Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map challenge. We want to build more than a map. Our idea is a Mars survival planner that shows safe routes, terrain hazards, water ice locations and dust storm risk, so future explorers can plan where to land, travel and set up base.
summary: Marsline is a tablet survival map for the first people walking on Mars. Before a crew leaves the habitat, they must know where it is safe to walk, how long it will take, and when to go. Marsline answers all three. We combined data from four orbiters (MRO, Mars Express, Mars Odyssey, Mars Global Surveyor) and the USGS geologic map into 13 layers on one 75 m grid of Jezero Crater, and engineered a three-class safety rating: nominal, caution and no-go. An A* planner gives routes with distance, walking time, climb and slope, and a spacewalk-window calculator uses real Perseverance weather to find safe start times. We tested the map against all 46 km of real Perseverance drives: none lies on our no-go ground, and the test caught and fixed a flaw in our first version. The tablet Live mission screen shows the crew’s longitude and latitude, weather with a satellite view, and additional routes (detour, shelter or new target) when a dust storm or blocked ground threatens the plan. The route walked is saved, with the surface and conditions, for the next crew member. The wrist display was removed. It matters because the first excursions will be a few kilometres on foot, and a crew needs decisions, not just pictures. Live values are simulated on real weather data. Marsline is a research concept, not mission software, and every assumption is shown on screen. All code and data are open.
details:
MARSLINE: A TABLET SURVIVAL MAP FOR THE FIRST PEOPLE WALKING ON MARS

Terrain-aware routes, spacewalk timing, live conditions and saved traverses for the Jezero Crater region

Team MartianPR · Poorna Weerasekara and Randula Hettiarachchi

NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 · Colombo · Challenge: Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map

15 November 2026 · Code: github.com/Randula2003/marsline

NOTE: lines in [square brackets] show where to insert an image in the editor (use Insert > Image). The file names are in the Marsline_Images folder.

ABSTRACT

The first astronauts on Mars will walk a few kilometres, not across a planet, yet most maps of Mars show the planet in broad strokes. A walker needs to know three things at once: where it is safe to go, how long it takes, and when to go. Marsline answers all three on a tablet. We combined data from four orbiters (Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, Mars Express, Mars Odyssey and Mars Global Surveyor) with the USGS geologic map of Jezero Crater, and engineered a 13-layer, 75-metre map with a three-class safety rating (nominal, caution, no-go). An A* route planner turns that map into a route with distance, time, slope and climb, and a spacewalk-window calculator uses real Perseverance weather measurements to find when a walk fits in daylight and above a chosen temperature. We tested the map against reality: none of the 46 km that Perseverance has driven (541 segments, to sol 2022) lies on our no-go ground, and the test exposed, and let us fix, a flaw in our first version. In this release the interface is a tablet crew display: the earlier wrist display is removed, and a Live mission screen shows the crew's longitude and latitude, the weather at the crew, a satellite view with a dust storm, additional routes (a detour, a shelter route or a new target) when a storm or hazard blocks the plan, and a saved handoff of the route walked, the hazards and the surface conditions for the next crew member. The live values are a simulation built on real Perseverance weather samples, because no live weather feed exists for Jezero. Marsline is a research concept, not mission software; every assumption is stated on screen and in this paper.

Keywords: Mars · Jezero Crater · traversability · route planning · A* · spacewalk planning · MEDA · tablet · NASA Space Apps

1. INTRODUCTION

1.1 The problem

People who walk on Mars will leave a habitat for hours, wearing a spacesuit, with a limited supply of air, power and daylight. Before they step out, someone has to answer one question: where is it safe to walk, and when? Global maps of Mars are made for scientists studying the whole planet. A walker needs a map of a few kilometres around them, with the ground rated for safety, a route, a time, and a window in the day to go.

1.2 Our answer

Marsline is a web application that runs on a tablet. It layers real orbital data on one shared grid, rates every 75-metre cell of the ground, plans routes over it, and tells the crew when to go. We built it for the NASA Space Apps Challenge Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map and focused on the Jezero Crater region, where Perseverance landed, because it has detailed data and a real rover path that we could use to test our map.

1.3 Contributions

• A 13-layer survival map of Jezero Crater (9 image layers and 4 vector overlays) on one 75 m grid, built from NASA, ESA and USGS data by a documented feature-engineering notebook.

• A three-class safety rating (nominal, caution, no-go) from slope, roughness and geology, and an A* route planner that gives distance, walking time, climb, maximum slope and the share of caution ground.

• A spacewalk-window calculator that combines the sun's position with real Perseverance MEDA temperatures to say when a walk fits in daylight and above a temperature limit that the crew sets.

• A reality check against all 541 real Perseverance drive segments (46 km). The check found a flaw in our first map, which we fixed and re-tested.

• A tablet Live mission screen with the crew's longitude and latitude, weather at the crew, a satellite view with a simulated dust storm, additional routes when a storm or hazard blocks the plan, and a saved handoff (route walked, hazards, surface conditions and notes) for the next crew member. The wrist display was removed.

• Open data and open code, with every limit and assumption stated in the app and in this paper.

1.4 Terms used in this paper

Short glossary. Every term is explained here once and used in the same way throughout.

Columns: Term | Meaning

• Sol: One Martian day, about 24 hours 39 minutes. Perseverance sol 410 is its 410th Martian day.

• Slope: How steep the ground is, in degrees. 0° is flat, 45° is a 100% grade.

• Roughness: How uneven the ground is: the local spread of height after the broad trend is removed. Rocky ground has a high value.

• Traversability: How safe it is to walk on a cell: nominal (fine), caution (slow or risky) or no-go (too steep).

• A* (A-star): A standard search method that finds the cheapest path across a grid of costs.

• MEDA: Mars Environmental Dynamics Analyzer, the weather station on Perseverance. It measures air temperature, pressure, wind and more.

• LMST, Ls: LMST is local mean solar time (the Mars clock at a place). Ls is solar longitude: where Mars is in its year, which sets the season.

• Spacewalk window: The range of start times for which a walk stays in daylight and above a chosen temperature.

• Traverse: The path someone walked (or a rover drove) from one place to another.

• Dust (sand) storm: A cloud of fine dust raised by wind. On Mars it mainly cuts visibility and sunlight (see section 5.3).

2. DATA

Every layer in Marsline comes from public NASA, ESA or USGS data. Nothing in the map is invented; where we had to assume something (such as how fast a person walks), we say so. Table 1 lists the data that the app uses and what each dataset is used for.

Table 1. Datasets used by Marsline.

Columns: Dataset | Source | Resolution | How Marsline uses it

• Digital terrain model from the Mars Express HRSC camera | ESA / DLR, via USGS | 75 m | Elevation, hillshade, slope, roughness, traversability, walking cost, elevation profile, atmospheric-depth layer

• Context Camera (CTX) mosaic | NASA / JPL, Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (Caltech mosaic) | 5 m (shown at 20 m) | Optical base layer (the satellite picture); 3 km previews of the science targets

• THEMIS day and night infrared mosaics | NASA / JPL, Mars Odyssey (USGS mosaic) | 100 m | Thermal layers (rock and sand show differently at night)

• Geologic map of Jezero crater and Nili Fossae (SIM 3464) | USGS Astrogeology | 1:75,000 | 14 geologic units, ridge and rim lines, 341 craters, landing ellipse; walking cost and science score; the 7 science targets

• MOLA global elevation | NASA / GSFC, Mars Global Surveyor | 463 m | Three regional study areas; independent check of the HRSC elevation

• Perseverance MEDA measurements and product index | NASA PDS Atmospheres Node | hourly medians for 4 sols | Weather charts; sun position and season; temperature limit; equation of time

• Perseverance raw images (Mastcam-Z, Navcam) | NASA / JPL-Caltech | 800 px previews | Ground-level view of the terrain

• Perseverance traverse (every real drive) | NASA / JPL, public MMGIS layers | 10 m sampling, 541 segments | Reality check of the map and the planner

• Published radiation measurements | Hassler et al. 2014; Zeitlin et al. 2013 | dose rates | Context only, never a crew dose

Figure 1. The four study areas in Marsline, shown as hillshade. Jezero Crater is detailed (75 m cells); Nili Fossae, Syrtis Major and Isidis Planitia are regional (463 m cells, from MOLA). Image data: ESA, NASA, USGS; hillshade computed by us.

3. FEATURE ENGINEERING

Raw satellite files cannot tell a walker where to go. We turned them into features: new layers that measure what matters for walking. This work is done once, offline, in a documented Python notebook (01_feature_engineering). The notebook writes small image and data files that the app loads in the browser (Figure 2).

Figure 2. From raw orbital data to the tablet app. Feature engineering is done offline; the app only loads the finished layers. Diagram drawn by the team.

3.1 One shared grid

The USGS map and its rasters use the Mars transverse Mercator projection (central meridian 77.5° E). We analyse in metres on that projection and warp every layer onto one longitude/latitude grid of 756 × 792 cells, 75 m each, covering 76.80°–77.80° E and 17.70°–18.70° N (about 57 × 59 km). Because the layers share one grid, they line up exactly and any point can be read from all of them at once. Longitude is east-positive on the Mars 2000 sphere.

3.2 Slope and roughness

Slope is computed from the HRSC elevation model with Horn's method, the same 3 × 3 finite-difference method used by GDAL and ArcGIS (Horn, 1981). Roughness is the local standard deviation of elevation after removing the broad trend, a proxy for rocky or uneven ground. Elevation in the study area runs from −3097 m to −1413 m.

3.3 Geology becomes a walking cost

The USGS map gives 14 geologic units. We assign each unit a walking-cost multiplier (loose sand and rugged ground are slower) and a science score (how interesting the unit is). These tables are concept assumptions, written in the notebook with the reason for each value, and they are not NASA-certified values. The seven science targets are placed in the highest-scoring units, at the point deepest inside the unit that is still walkable (Table 2).

Table 2. The seven science targets chosen from the geologic units.

Columns: Target | Unit | Science score | Slope at target

• T1 Jezero fan 1 | Jezero fan 1 unit | 1.00 | 0.2°

• T2 Jezero fan 2 | Jezero fan 2 unit | 0.95 | 3.8°

• T4 Upper etched | Upper etched unit | 0.80 | 1.0°

• T5 Lower etched | Lower etched unit | 0.80 | 1.6°

• T3 Nili Planum fan | Nili Planum fan unit | 0.70 | 4.7°

• T7 Crater rim | Crater rim unit | 0.70 | 6.0°

• T6 Jezero floor | Jezero floor unit | 0.65 | 0.7°

3.4 Traversability classes and route cost

Every cell gets one of three classes. The limits are concept assumptions, not mobility limits of a real spacesuit:

• No-go: slope of 25° or more.

• Caution: slope of 15° or more, roughness of 3 m or more, geology cost of 1.5× or more, or a ridge, rim or delta-front line.

• Nominal: everything else.

The cost of walking across a cell combines all three features:

route cost = geology cost × (1 + (slope / 15°)²) × (1 + roughness / 3 m)

No-go cells are blocked completely. Across the Jezero area the ground divides into 67.7% nominal, 31.7% caution and 0.6% no-go.

Figure 3. The engineered layers of Marsline for Jezero Crater, all on the same 75 m grid. A: CTX optical mosaic (NASA/JPL/MSSS, Caltech). B: HRSC hillshade (ESA/DLR/FU Berlin; USGS). C: slope derived by us. D: THEMIS night infrared (NASA/JPL/ASU). E: our traversability classes. F: science score. G: atmospheric depth (radiation context, derived from elevation).

3.5 Vector overlays and the browser data texture

Four vector overlays come straight from the USGS database and are reprojected to longitude and latitude: geologic units (14), linear features (ridges, rim crests, delta fronts and channels; 382 lines), craters (341) and the landing ellipse. Together with the nine image layers they make the app's 13 layers. For the route planner, slope, route cost and class are packed into one small image, a data texture, that the browser decodes into arrays (slope × 4, cost × 40 and class in the red, green and blue channels).

3.6 Cross-check against an independent elevation model

HRSC is local and sharp, while MOLA is the global reference. If both agree on absolute elevation the layers can be trusted. They agree closely: correlation 0.995, mean difference 3.3 m and RMS difference 30.8 m.

3.7 More study areas

The same method applied to the MOLA tile gives three regional areas (Nili Fossae, Syrtis Major, Isidis Planitia). They have hillshade, slope, traversability, relief-derived targets and routes, but no geologic map or optical imagery, and the 463 m cells smooth the slopes. The app marks them as regional and uses stricter slope limits (8° caution and 15° no-go, set in the notebook) because the coarse cells hide steep ground.

3.8 Weather features

We downloaded Perseverance MEDA measurements for four sols, one per season (51, 247, 410 and 552 in Mars year 36), and reduced them to hourly medians of local mean solar time. From the files we also measured the equation of time, the difference between true and mean solar time, which moves the sunrise and sunset. Local air temperature across these sols ranges from −82 °C to −9 °C and air pressure from 646 to 776 Pa (Figure 4).

Figure 4. Real Perseverance MEDA measurements: hourly median air temperature and air pressure against local mean solar time, for one sample sol in each season (NASA PDS, Mars 2020 MEDA derived data; plotted by us).

4. ROUTE PLANNING AND SPACEWALK TIMING

4.1 A* route planner

The planner runs in the browser. It searches the 75 m grid with A*, moving to the eight neighbouring cells, never cutting a corner through a no-go cell, and never entering a no-go cell. The cost of a step is its length multiplied by the mean route cost of the two cells, so the planner prefers easy ground and accepts a longer way round steep or rough ground. The estimate of the remaining distance is the straight-line (octile) distance, which never overestimates, so the route found is the cheapest one (Hart, Nilsson and Raphael, 1968). Walking time assumes 3 km/h on easy ground, scaled by the cost of each step. The crew can change the speed, the no-go slope (tighten only) and the spacewalk limit to see the effect.

For every route the app reports distance, walking time, climb and descent, maximum and mean slope, the share on caution ground, the straight-line distance, whether the straight line is blocked, and an elevation profile (Figure 5).

Figure 5. One-page mission map generated by the notebook: CTX imagery with the safety layer, geologic boundaries, the seven science targets and two example routes. Route A (base to T1) is 13.9 km, about 7 h 11 min of walking, maximum slope 8.0°, 6% on caution ground. Route B (base to T2) is 3.3 km, about 2 h, maximum slope 4.4°, 6% on caution ground. Slope limits and walking speed are concept assumptions.

4.2 Spacewalk window

A route says where and how long, but not when. For a chosen season, Marsline computes the sun's elevation through the Martian day from the latitude and solar longitude:

sin(elevation) = sin(latitude)·sin(declination) + cos(latitude)·cos(declination)·cos(hour angle), declination = asin( sin(25.19°) · sin(Ls) )

It corrects the clock with the equation of time measured from the MEDA files, then tests every start time in 15-minute steps. A start time is allowed if the sun stays above the horizon for the whole round trip and the measured air temperature never falls below a limit that the crew chooses (the default is −55 °C and is not a real suit specification). For the 3.3 km walk to fan 2 and back, about 4.2 hours, in spring, any start between 08:30 and 14:15 local mean solar time works, and the best start is 12:45. In winter the window is shorter, 09:45 to 13:45. A 14 km round trip is longer than the daylight, so the app tells the crew to split it into several excursions.

Figure 6. The spacewalk-window panel in the app (screenshot): season tabs, temperature limit, the recommended start times and a day chart. Cream is daylight, blue is measured air temperature, green is the recommended walk.

4.3 Additional routes around storms and hazards

When a dust storm or a hazard marker threatens the plan, Marsline plans up to three additional routes from the crew's current position. All of them keep out of the storm and hazard zones, which are circles that the planner treats as closed ground:

• Detour: a route to the same destination that avoids the zones.

• Shelter: the quickest route to a shelter (the base or a saved habitat waypoint).

• New target: the nearest other science target that can still be reached. This is offered only when the chosen destination is unreachable.

A destination inside a zone cannot be reached, and the app says so. If the crew is already inside a zone, the zone is made expensive instead of closed (six times the normal cost), so that the planner can lead the crew out of it. The crew chooses; the app never switches route by itself, and every change is written to the mission feed.

5. THE PRODUCT: MARSLINE ON A TABLET

5.1 Architecture

Marsline is a single Next.js 16 and React 19 application written in TypeScript. The map is a custom canvas that pans, zooms and pinches with touch, so it works on a tablet. The workspace (waypoints, mission log, simulated life-support values and messages) is stored in Cloud Firestore behind server routes that check a Firebase Authentication token; each user's data is kept under their own user ID, and Firestore rules deny direct browser access. If Firebase is not configured, the app switches to a demo mode that keeps the same data in the browser, so every feature still works. The app can be installed as a web app (manifest and service worker), and its data layers load from files stored with the app. The repository includes 49 automated tests (data files, terrain, route planner, spacewalk window, live mission, hazard avoidance and handoff records); all of them pass on the version described here.

5.2 Screens

• Surface map. Four study areas, 13 switchable layers, an opacity slider and a hover readout that shows latitude, longitude, elevation, slope, class and rock unit. Tapping a target or waypoint sets the destination, and pick A/B on map sets any point.

• Route planner. Distance, time, climb, slopes and caution share, a straight-line comparison, a warning if the walk is longer than the spacewalk limit, and Save route to mission.

• Spacewalk window. The calculator described in section 4.2.

• Current conditions. Real MEDA weather charts for four seasons, real Perseverance photos, and live retrieval of the NASA PDS product indexes (these list which data products exist; they are not measurements).

• Live mission. The tablet crew display described in section 5.3.

• Science data layers and Datasets used. A catalogue of every dataset, where it came from, how it is used and its credit.

• Radiation context, life support, communications and mission log. Published radiation values shown as context only; simulated life-support values; a simulated message outbox; a log of observations and route updates. All simulated values are labelled as such.

Figure 7. The Surface map in the app (screenshot, tablet size): satellite base layer with the safety overlay, ridge and crater overlays, science targets, four study areas and switchable data layers.

Figure 8. What the ground looks like: raw Mastcam-Z image from Perseverance, sol 410 (NASA/JPL-Caltech/ASU). The app shows real rover photos beside the orbital layers.

Figure 8a. The route planner in the app (screenshot): a terrain-aware A* route from the landing site to Jezero fan 1 with distance, walking time, climb, slopes, share of caution ground and the elevation profile.

Figure 8b. The Checks panel in the app (screenshot): the reality check against real Perseverance drives.

Figure 8c. Current conditions page in the app (screenshot): real Perseverance MEDA weather charts and the weather table.

Figure 8d. Datasets used page in the app (screenshot): every dataset with its source, resolution, use and credit.

5.3 New in this release: the tablet Live mission screen

This release makes the tablet the product. The wrist interface (wristband display) of the earlier version has been removed: a wrist-sized screen is too small to show a map with layers and routes, so the crew display is a tablet, with large readouts and touch controls. The new Live mission screen follows the workflow in Figure 9 and is shown in Figures 10 to 12.

Figure 9. The field workflow of the Live mission screen. This is a schematic of the functions, drawn by the team.

1. Live mission and condition update. A banner shows the condition level (nominal, advisory, warning or storm) with a one-line instruction, and the local solar time. A live feed lists every change, such as Dust front detected, Route changed or Arrived. The clock runs at 1×, 4× or 10× simulated speed.

2. Position and weather with a satellite view. The crew's position is shown as longitude and latitude (five decimals, east-positive). A weather card shows air temperature, wind and gust, pressure, dust opacity, visibility and the distance to the storm edge. Below them, the map shows orbital (CTX) imagery with the crew's position, the routes and the dust cloud.

3. Additional routes for a sand (dust) storm or unreachable ground. When a storm or hazard threatens the route, or the destination cannot be reached, the app offers a detour, a shelter route or a new target (section 4.3). The crew can also mark a hazard at their position.

4. The route walked is saved. While the crew walks, the app records their trail (a point about every 30 m, at most 600 points) and keeps it across a reload of the page.

5. The route and the surface are saved for the next comer. When a traverse ends, a handoff record is saved automatically, and the crew can save one at any time with notes. A record holds the route walked, the planned and the alternate route, the hazard markers, the storm, the surface and weather conditions at that moment, and the crew's notes. The next crew member opens it from the list of previous handoffs, and sees the earlier trail, hazards and last position on the map.

Figure 10. The Live mission screen on a tablet (screenshot): condition banner and local solar time, the crew's longitude and latitude, weather at the crew, and the live mission feed.

Figure 11. A dust storm approaching (screenshot). The satellite map shows the crew, the planned route to T1 and the simulated dust cloud. The panel offers two additional routes: a detour to T1 and a shelter route, each with distance, time and maximum slope.

Figure 12. Saving for the next crew member (screenshot): the notes box, the saved handoffs and the additional routes. The crew took the shelter route and a handoff was saved when the traverse ended.

Figure 12b. The Live mission screen at tablet portrait size (screenshot).

How the storm simulation works. The storm is a scenario that the operator switches on (clear, approaching or inside), so that the app can show how the routes react. In the approaching scenario a front forms to the north-west and moves toward the crew. The condition level depends on the distance to the storm edge (Table 4), and conditions worsen smoothly as the front approaches.

Table 4. Condition levels of the storm simulation. The values are concept assumptions, not measurements.

Columns: Level | When | Message to the crew

• NOMINAL | No storm, or more than 30 km from its edge | No hazard detected. Continue the planned traverse.

• ADVISORY | Edge within 30 km (or a storm moving away) | A dust front is in range. Keep the alternate route ready.

• WARNING | Edge within 10 km | Visibility will drop soon. Take the detour or shelter route now.

• STORM | Crew inside the storm | Visibility is poor. Move to shelter and report your position.

Baseline temperature, pressure and wind come from a real Perseverance MEDA sample sol. The simulation then raises the dust opacity from 0.5 (clear sky) to 3.5 (storm), lowers the daytime temperature by up to 18 °C, raises the wind, and estimates visibility as 12.5 km divided by the opacity. These values are assumptions. The local solar time is computed from the real clock with the Mars24 algorithm (Allison and McEwen, 2000).

Sand storms on Mars. What people call a Martian sand storm is a dust storm: the grains are very fine. The air at the surface is extremely thin (we measured 646–776 Pa at Jezero, under 1% of Earth's sea-level pressure), so wind of a given speed pushes far less than on Earth. The real dangers of a dust storm are poor visibility, less sunlight for solar power, and dust on equipment. That is why Marsline treats a storm as a reason to change the route or return to shelter.

What is real and what is simulated. Real: the Perseverance MEDA baseline for temperature, pressure and wind; the orbital imagery; the HRSC terrain; the route planning. Simulated: the crew's position, the dust storm and the live feed. No live weather feed exists for Jezero, and a tablet cannot get a GPS fix on Mars; a real system would use rover or beacon fixes. The app states this on the Live mission screen.

6. VALIDATION: IS THE MAP RIGHT?

Hazard maps usually come with a confidence statement, not a test. NASA publishes every drive that Perseverance has made, so we could test our map against reality. We laid the rover's path over our safety map and compared it with our planner (Figure 13, Table 3).

Figure 13. Left: every real Perseverance drive (sol 14 to 2022) over our safety map. Right: the slopes the rover chose to cross compared with the whole area; the dashed lines are our caution (15°) and no-go (25°) limits. Rover path: NASA/JPL, public MMGIS layers.

Table 3. Validation results against real Perseverance drives.

Columns: Measure | Result

• Drive segments in the study area: 541 segments, 46.0 km, sol 14 to 2022, sampled every 10 m

• Share of the rover path on our no-go ground: 0.0% (our no-go ground is 0.6% of the area)

• Share of the rover path on caution / nominal ground: 45.3% caution, 54.7% nominal (the area is 31.7% caution, 67.7% nominal)

• Slope under the rover path: median 3.8°, 95th percentile 14.7°, maximum 19.7° (our no-go limit is 25°)

• Our planner against 70 real drives: route length is a median 0.91 of the real length (middle half 0.83–1.05); 80% of routes within 25% of the real length

• HRSC against MOLA elevation: correlation 0.995, RMS difference 30.8 m

The test caught a mistake. Our first map treated ridge, rim and delta-front lines as impassable, yet 12.0% of the real drive path lay on them, all on slopes under 20°. We changed those lines to high-cost caution ground and re-ran the check. The result above is for the corrected map. This is why we trust the map more than a map that was only drawn.

What the test does not show. The rover has different mobility limits than a person on foot, and the drives were chosen by JPL planners. Agreement shows that our map is consistent with real drive planning, not that it is proven safe for crew. Our grid is 75 m, and rover localisation and the elevation model have their own errors.

7. RESULTS AT A GLANCE

Table 5. Key results of the project.

Columns: Item | Result

• Study area: Jezero Crater and delta, 57 × 59 km, 75 m cells (756 × 792), plus three regional areas at 463 m

• Layers: 13: 9 image layers and 4 vector overlays

• Ground classes: 67.7% nominal, 31.7% caution, 0.6% no-go

• Example route A (base to T1, Jezero fan 1): 13.9 km, about 7 h 11 min, max slope 8.0°, 6% on caution ground

• Example route B (base to T2, Jezero fan 2): 3.3 km, about 2 h, max slope 4.4°, 6% on caution ground

• Spacewalk window, route B round trip, spring: start between 08:30 and 14:15 (local mean solar time); best 12:45

• Measured weather (Perseverance MEDA): air −82 to −9 °C; pressure 646–776 Pa

• Reality check: 0.0% of 46 km of real drives on no-go ground; planner length ratio 0.91

• Tablet Live mission screen: crew longitude and latitude, weather at the crew, satellite view with a simulated dust storm, additional routes (detour, shelter, new target), saved handoff for the next crew member

• Automated tests: 49, all passing

8. LIMITATIONS AND RESPONSIBLE USE

• Marsline is not mission software and is not validated for crew operations. It shows how real data, tested against reality, can turn a map into a decision.

• A rover is not an astronaut. Our validation uses rover drives. Slope limits (15° caution, 25° no-go), the walking speed and the geology costs are concept assumptions, and the crew can change them. Real spacesuit mobility limits are not yet included.

• The weather is four sample days, one per season. Day-to-day variation, dust storms and instrument flags are not represented in the charts.

• The three regional areas are coarse (463 m cells), so their slopes are smoothed and their targets are relief-derived candidates that need checking with higher-resolution images.

• The live mission values are simulated. The crew position, the dust storm and the live feed are simulations. The storm levels, dust opacity, visibility and cooling are concept assumptions. A tablet cannot get a GPS fix on Mars.

• Radiation is shown as published context, not a crew dose. Life-support values and communications are simulations; no radio transmission takes place.

• Orbital pictures are archived data. They show the ground as it was when the orbiter imaged it, not a live view.

• Longitude is east-positive on the Mars 2000 sphere. Coordinates from other conventions must be converted before use.

3. Hassler, D. M., et al. (2014). Mars' surface radiation environment measured with the Mars Science Laboratory's Curiosity rover. Science, 343(6169), 1244797.

4. Horn, B. K. P. (1981). Hill shading and the reflectance map. Proceedings of the IEEE, 69(1), 14–47.
